Corner Rest Machining
Optimized removal of rest material in vertical corners and adjacent bottom surfaces within pocket and
pocket-like geometries with constant corner radii.
This cycle is not designed for use on complex 3D free-form geometries. The 5X Rest
Machining cycle is provided for this.
The cycle offers the functions of the 3D Corner Rest Machining cycle as well as an additional indexed
corner machining function in which the optimal tool inclination is calculated for each corner (A). This means
that there is no need to manually define individual frames for individual corners.
This function is also available for the Bullnose End Mill, Radiusmill tool type.
• Optimized strategies for corners (B), rest material (C) and floor areas (D), depending on the machin-
ing situation and the model geometry.
• Protects the upper model edges with an automatic milling surface extension (1).
• Parallel machining with high-volume material removed in the area of vertical corners (2)
• Z Level Machining with low-volume material removed for rest material close to the bottom (3)
• Machining of the border areas of bottom surfaces that are adjacent to the rest material (4)
• Seamless transitions between the machining areas and to the side and bottom surfaces through
smooth overlapping of the toolpaths (5).

Free Path Milling
Free Path Milling performs collision-checked machining along a freely specifiable center point path with a
multiple axial infeed. It is possible to machine undercuts.
Tool
If the Tip option is selected in the tool panel, then the toolpath is output offset in the axial direction in
relation to the contour. The tool is always kept on the guiding contour with a center reference, irrespective
of the reference point setting for the path output in the tool panel.
Contours
Tool position: In contrast to 3D Free Path Milling, milling to the right or left of the contour is not possible in
5X Free Path Machining.
Contour selection
The following can be selected as machining contours: arcs, circles, reference lines, curves and edge
curves of surfaces. Several contours or holes can be machined in one job. The number of selected
contours is displayed.

in this contour list, you can quickly define the same top and bottom values for several contours.

Setup
As is the case for 3D Machining of free curves, a 3DF file is only required for 5-axis curve machining when
a collision check needs to be performed.
Model
Specify the model (milling area) required for the current job.
Multiple allowances: If the milling area contains groups with different allowances, these allowances are
taken into account during machining if the function is enabled.
Additional surfaces: temporary safety surfaces to avoid unnecessary rapid travel movements. Surfa-
ces in the machining area that need to be known to perform a correct collision check.
Check tool
The tool check ensures that all of the components defined for the tool are protected from a possible
collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.
Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.
Tool check setup: the tool check settings are specified in this dialog box. For further information, see
section Tool check setup (page 1163)
If no collisions occur for the model (3DF file), then the tool center point always moves on the contour.
The collision check for the 3DF file causes the milling tool to be retracted axially taking into account the
specified allowance until there is no longer a collision. To machine undercuts, place center point paths in
the undercut area behind the surface.

Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:
• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).
Clip: The toolpath is fully calculated. Only the collision-free areas of the toolpaths are output. As a result of
rework machining with another tool and/or another tool inclination, the toolpaths found in the collision can
be tracked and checked for collisions (applies to all 3D machining strategies).
Collision avoidance: With this option, the tool is side-stepped to avoid collision so that the material can be
machined as deeply as possible with the most robust possible tool.
The toolpaths calculated for the Clip option are used as the basis for the 3D Rework Machining cycle.
An area is determined and graphically displayed within the 3D Automatic Rest Machining cycle. Any further
machining occurs within the following cycle only: 3D Automatic Rest Machining.
When the Collision avoidance function is used, a milling area that is not within the stock is also protected
against collisions. If the milling area that is outside of the stock only consists of perpendicular surfaces, no
collision avoidance takes place; instead, the milling path output is suppressed.
Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Angle difference for various tool inclinations between two separate machining areas
(for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance
distance is defined as the retract mode (Parameters dialog page) (1).
If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the
clearance distance (dialog page: Parameters) (2). If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to
clearance distance. If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to clearance distance.
Clearance straighten angle: If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of
the tool is greater than the defined straighten angle (default = 45°), the tool turns to the defined value for
the straighten angle, after it has reached the clearance plane.
If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of the tool is smaller than or
equal to the defined Straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
inclination (3).

Macros
Additional movements to vertical infeed and retract movements that define a gentle approach and retract
behavior at the calculated milling paths.
Macros are only executed if they do not result in a collision with neighboring surfaces.
Macro mode
Macros can be defined manually or calculated automatically by
hyperMILL.
Automatic
Smooth: The approach or retract movement is performed smoothly in a circular motion.
Length: Defines the length of the approach or retract movement.
Side clearance/Axial clearance: Clearance in the axial or X/Y direction that can be travelled without a
collision.
Max. axial lift: Maximum lifting movement in the axial direction.
Manual
The tool is approached or retracted either in a Perpendicular, Circular or Tangential manner.
The retraction can also be performed as a Ramp. These additional movements are only ever performed if
they do not result in a collision with neighboring surfaces.
Approach macro / Retract macro
Approach macros/retract macros are additional movements during infeed to the first milling path or during
retraction after the last milling path.
Vertical (1): Linear movement in the direction of the tool axis. Enter length.
Circular (2): Approach and retract movements are performed in a quarter circle. Enter radius of the circle.
Tangential (3): Approach and retract movements are performed on the machining plane along the contour
tangent. Enter length.
Ramp (4): Approach macro only. Soft cutting along the path.

Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.

For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:
• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).

The following infeed strategies are available:
Along axis (1): The toolpaths run along the X axis.
Radial (normal to axis) (2): The toolpaths run perpendicular to the X axis.

Rule (6) / Flow (7): Two guide curves (A) that do not overlap and that have the same direction should be

curve is treated as the positive X axis.

Horizontal infeed mode
The horizontal infeed mode defines the mode of computation for the distances between the individual
milling paths.
The computation of the path distance for ruled profiles and flow profiles can be controlled via user-defined
synchronization lines.
Constant stepover (1): Infeed with fixed horizontal increment. The vertical distance between the toolpaths
(Z-Levels) is constant for all Z-levels Specify the horizontal stepover. Machining of steep surfaces causes
steps in the surface. Possible remedies: Machining at an angle (turning the workpiece around the Z axis)
Select Scallop height infeed mode. For round parts select one of the guide curve strategies.
Scallop height (2): Machining is only possible with ball mills. A predefined scallop height is not exceeded
even on steep side surfaces. The Z-distance between the individual milling paths depends on the surface
curvature and steepness. The complete Z-level is taken into consideration and the smallest value found is
used to determine the stepdown.
Scallop height value: Enter the required scallop height. The Scallop height infeed mode will significantly
increase the calculation time for the milling paths.
CAM
1199

-- 1199 of 1632 --

1 	2
Minimum horizontal stepover: Limits the distance between the milling paths. Avoids machining that is too
fine when the required scallop height cannot be reached because of very steep side surfaces. Apply this
for machining areas with steep side surfaces (surface slope > 50°) and very smooth surfaces.
Constant on curve projection: A guide curve (1) is projected onto the surfaces and stepped equally on the
basis of the specified infeed. This significantly improves surface quality. The minimum horizontal stepover
limits the distance of the paths, particularly in steep areas. Only one profile (spline, line, curve) can be
defined. Vertical surfaces cannot be machined.

Retract mode
The retract mode defines the Z level where the system executes horizontal infeed movements.
The mode set is valid for all machining directions (incl. approach, retract and return movement macros)
and for the profiles machined with them. Exception: Machining in zigzag mode without return macro.
Clearance distance : all retract and infeed movements are executed via the clearance distance. Starting
and end positions of an infeed movement in rapid are displaced in Z direction in order to guarantee a
collision-free linear infeed movement. The clearance distance is added to these positions.
Clearance plane : all retract and infeed movements are executed via the clearance plane.

Undercut behavior

stopped if necessary.

possible. Using this option allows rest material to remain in the model.

Mode
Limit the machining area in the horizontal direction.
Boundaries: Closed curves can be used as boundaries, for example, Polylines (2D/3D), Splines, Cir-
cles. The Z-position of the boundary is not considered during calculation of the machining area. 3D curves
are projected into the XY plane.
Tool reference
Define the machining area with reference to the boundary curve.
Toward (1): Machining ends as soon as there is contact between the tool shank and the boundary (1).
On (2): Machining until the tool axis is on top of the boundary.
Past (3): The tool axis leaves the boundary. Machining ends as soon as there is no longer contact
between the tool shank and the boundary.

Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool

Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Angle difference for various tool inclinations between two separate machining areas
(for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance
distance is defined as the retract mode (Parameters dialog page).
If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the
clearance distance (Parameters dialog page). Here, the feedrate for clearance movements is used. If there
is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to clearance distance.
Clearance straighten angle: If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of
the tool is greater than the defined straighten angle (default = 45°), the tool turns to the defined value for
the straighten angle, after it has reached the clearance plane.
If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of the tool is smaller than or
equal to the defined straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
inclination.
The clearance straighten angle provides collision avoidance, especially on machines with conical interpola-
tion that allow a 180° vector change.
The straighten angle must be defined so that the tip of the tool describes the deepest
point of the entire collision body, including spindle and head. The Z axis of the frame
must be parallel to the Z axis of the NCS.

Clearance feedrate: Linking movements between two machining areas in the clearance distance are
executed at this feedrate.
Condition for retraction to clearance plane:
Clearance plane is defined as retract mode or value for Clearance straighten angle is exceeded (as
described above).

close to the surface with machining feedrate (G1). In the case where gaps are greater than the maximum
gap distance, and depending on the settings for the retract mode in the Machining parameters menu, the
system executes a retraction movement to the clearance distance or clearance plane, with a subsequent
infeed movement to the next surface in rapid.

dialog under Machine properties → General → Virtual Machine directory by clicking the icon
and configure the stop of the tool in the NC → General → Output area with the available
options.
High precision surface mode: Enable if the highest accuracy is required to calculate the toolpath (Machin-
ing tolerance ≤ 0.005). Here, calculation of the toolpath is not based on the faceted model geometry but on
the real surfaces of the model.

To generate the toolpaths, cuts are made along a central curve. Compared to the tube cycles, the tool axis
does not run along the central curve, but more or less perpendicular to it.

Infinite (4).

Synchronize toolpaths
Synchronization lines Synchronization lines run between the two boundaries or between the boundary and
the upper curve. They are to be used to divide the halfpipe into areas and so influence the course of
slicing as well as the course of the paths running across. The interpolation of the slices/paths then takes
place – as with other machining strategies – over the areas limited by the synchronization lines. Slicing
improvements improve the quality of the toolpaths – including those along the halfpipe.

Tilt strategy
Prefer vertical: Tilt strategy for milling tools and moulds with demolding in the Z direction. For slight
undercuts, the machining can perform a 4X or 5X movement locally. This can be suppressed using the Tip
check tolerance (see the Setup dialog page).
Toward top curve: The tool axis is tilted at the specified angle in the direction of the upper curve. The
connection line between the upper and lower curve corresponds to 0 degrees.
Radial Z: The tool axis is aligned with the specified angle to the Z axis of the frame. If the Fixed tilt option is
activated, the swivel axis remains unchanged during collision avoidance. When the Always radial option is
selected, the tool axis is always aligned radially to the Z axis of the frame.

each of which is milled with a fixed tool inclination.

Additional movements to vertical infeed and retract movements that define a gentle approach and retract
behavior at the calculated milling paths.

Additional movements during infeed to the first milling path or during retraction after the last milling path of
machining. Radius and Axial offset can be defined separately for approach and retract.

Return macro / Linking movement
The retraction of the tool at the end of a path and the approach to the next path is referred to as a return
macro. Retraction and approach take place in one continuous movement. If defining the optional Radius,
small values should be given preference, particularly in narrow channels. If radius = 0, the return macro is
not executed and therefore the tool is not lifted from the component.
The two ends of the return macro are connected with a smooth movement (spline), for which a separate
Feedrate can be defined, which, as a rule, may be larger than the machining feedrate. For safety’s sake,
the increased feedrate is only carried out if the totalLinking movement (1) does not fall below the Min.
clearance to part.

Model
Specify the model (milling area) required for the current job.
Multiple allowances: If the milling area contains groups with different allowances, these allowances are
taken into account during machining if the function is enabled.
Additional surfaces: temporary safety surfaces to avoid unnecessary rapid travel movements. Surfa-
ces in the machining area that need to be known to perform a correct collision check.
Check tool
The tool check ensures that all of the components defined for the tool are protected from a possible
collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.
Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.
Tool check setup: the tool check settings are specified in this dialog box. For further information, see
section Tool check setup (page 1224)

Clearance value added for each tool component (retained minimum distance to model). The following tool
components are checked: 1. Spindle, 2. Holder, 3. Extension, 4. Thick shank (see image below). The tool
tip is checked without clearance.
When using machining cycles that work with stock models, the defined clearance distance may deviate
and will be increased if necessary.

Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:
• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).
Clip: The toolpath is fully calculated. Only the collision-free areas of the toolpaths are output. As a result of
rework machining with another tool and/or another tool inclination, the toolpaths found in the collision can
be tracked and checked for collisions (applies to all 3D machining strategies).
Collision avoidance: With this option, the tool is side-stepped to avoid collision so that the material can be
machined as deeply as possible with the most robust possible tool.
The toolpaths calculated for the Clip option are used as the basis for the 3D Rework Machining cycle.
An area is determined and graphically displayed within the 3D Automatic Rest Machining cycle. Any further
machining occurs within the following cycle only: 3D Automatic Rest Machining.
When the Collision avoidance function is used, a milling area that is not within the stock is also protected
against collisions. If the milling area that is outside of the stock only consists of perpendicular surfaces, no
collision avoidance takes place; instead, the milling path output is suppressed.
NC parameters
Machining tolerance: Enter the required machining tolerance. The value defines the accuracy with which
the calculation for the generation of the toolpaths is carried out.
Maximum G1 length(1): maximum length of the G1 movements on planar surfaces which are output in
the NC program. Greater distances are subdivided into a corresponding number of G1 movements of the
specified length. Controlling the G1 length avoids too strong accelerations of the machine on large planar
surfaces.
1
Min. G0 distance (1): Distance between two machining areas that can be traversed – without tool contact –
close to the surface with machining feedrate (G1). In the case where gaps are greater than the maximum
gap distance, and depending on the settings for the retract mode in the Machining parameters menu, the
system executes a retraction movement to the clearance distance or clearance plane, with a subsequent
infeed movement to the next surface in rapid.

Surface Milling
The cycles of the surface machining package are used for machining slightly curved surfaces and geome-
tries with regular surfaces.
The tool inclination is generally determined by the surface normals of the selected surface or guiding
surface.
All additional elements (points, lines, contours) that determine the milling behavior of the tool must lie on
the surfaces to be machined.
Overview of cycles
The cycles of the surface machining package are used for machining slightly curved surfaces and geome-
tries with regular surfaces.
The tool inclination is generally determined by the surface normals of the selected surface or guiding
surface.
All additional elements (points, lines, contours) that determine the milling behavior of the tool must lie on
the surfaces to be machined.
5X Top Milling (1):
Top Milling in which the tool inclination at the contact point is calculated with a freely specifiable slope
angle to the surface normals. The toolpaths can be oriented to the X or Y axis or to a freely definable
profile.
5X Iso Top Milling (2):
Here, the tool inclination at the contact point is calculated with a freely specifiable slope angle to the
normal of face in the infeed direction. The toolpaths are oriented to the U or V lines of the surface(s) or the
selected synchronization lines.

5X contour machining is particularly suited to shape elements that are milled with a defined tool inclination
to the surface, such as grooves, cut edges or engravings. Using optional synchronization lines, the tool

5X SWARF Cutting 1 Curve (4):
The cycle is used for regular surfaces that permit a milling tool to come into contact with a line. The
machining area in the axial direction is defined by a profile curve.
The tool inclination is determined by the surface to be milled. The use of end mills with swarf machining
enables short machining times.
5X SWARF Cutting 2 Curves (5):
The cycle is used for regular surfaces that permit a milling tool to come into contact with a line. For swarf
cutting with two curves, the machining area in the axial direction is also defined by a profile curve.
As opposed to swarf cutting with one curve, the tool inclination here is defined by an additional profile
curve. The use of end mills with swarf machining enables short machining times.

Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Angle difference for various tool inclinations between two separate machining areas
(for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance
distance is defined as the retract mode (Parameters dialog page) (1).
If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the
clearance distance (dialog page: Parameters) (2). If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to
clearance distance. If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to clearance distance.
Clearance straighten angle: If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of
the tool is greater than the defined straighten angle (default = 45°), the tool turns to the defined value for
the straighten angle, after it has reached the clearance plane.
If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of the tool is smaller than or
equal to the defined Straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
inclination (3).

Condition for retraction to clearance plane:

described above).

specified length. Controlling the G1 length avoids too strong accelerations of the machine on large planar
surfaces.

angle to the surface normal in the infeed direction. The toolpaths are oriented to the U or V lines of the
surface(s) or the selected synchronization lines.

Strategy
Strategy
Iso orientation: The milling paths follow the ISO lines (U, V) of the selected surfaces.
Global orientation: The milling paths follow the optimal machining direction automatically determined by
hyperMILL.
Example of use:
ISO orientation (1): many retract movements, and therefore not recommended for the example above.
Global orientation (2): few retract movements, and therefore the preferred machining strategy.
Surfaces: The area to be milled is defined by one or more selectable surfaces. This area can be limited
by optionally selecting a boundary. A guiding surface can be determined to optimize the tool inclination for
unfavorable surface profiles.
Machining direction
U parameter / V parameter: The machining direction is determined using U and V parameters. If more than
one surface is selected for machining, then they are only machined at one time if the corresponding U or V
parameters have the same orientation and do not indicate an offset.
Toolpath smoothing
Fillet interior corners: Milling paths at corners with sharp changes in direction are gently rounded with the
defined radius.

Tilt parameters
Desired lead angle: Angle by which the tool is tilted in the infeed direction. The angle is relative to the
normal vector of the surface.
Max. angle to Z: Maximum permitted angle of the tool to the Z axis of the frame.
4+1 machining
Fixed angle: Fix the tilt vector of the tool on one of the main axes of the frame (X, Y, Z). In addition, you
can optionally specify a slope angle to the axis (default = 90 degrees).
Retraction on collision
Distance control: This option causes the tool to retract if the distance between 3DF model and the selected
guiding surface exceeds the value specified under Max. gap distance.
Max. gap distance: Defines the machining area between 3DF model and guiding surface. If the tool is
required to retract further than defined under Max. gap distance, then this area is not machined.
If the value for the minimum distance G0 (settings) is less than or equal to the maximum distance, then the
area between 3DF model and guiding surface is traversed at working feedrate. If this value is greater than
the maximum distance, then rapid is used for retraction to the clearance distance or plane.
Macros
Approach macro / Retract macro
Approach macros/retract macros are additional movements during infeed to the first milling path or during
retraction after the last milling path.
Vertical (1): Linear movement in the direction of the tool axis. Enter length.
Circular (2): Approach and retract movements are performed in a quarter circle. Enter radius of the circle.
Tangential (3): Approach and retract movements are performed on the machining plane along the contour
tangent. Enter length.
Ramp (4): Approach macro only. Soft cutting along the path.

Model

Select the model (milling area) required for the current job.
Additional surfaces: temporary safety surfaces to avoid unnecessary rapid travel movements. Surfa-
ces in the machining area that need to be known to perform a correct collision check.
Check tool
The tool check ensures that all of the components defined for the tool are protected from a possible
collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.
Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.
Tool check setup: the tool check settings are specified in this dialog box. For further information, see
section Tool check setup (page 722)
Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
CAM
1242

-- 1242 of 1632 --

Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

Display calculated tool length
If the same tool is used in several jobs, the tool length calculated by
hyperMILL is displayed. In this
instance, after creating the toolpath file(s), select the tool in the browser and choose the Usage function on
the shortcut menu.
For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:
• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).
Clip: The toolpath is fully calculated. Only the collision-free areas of the toolpaths are output. As a result of
rework machining with another tool and/or another tool inclination, the toolpaths found in the collision can
be tracked and checked for collisions (applies to all 3D machining strategies).
Collision avoidance: With this option, the tool is side-stepped to avoid collision so that the material can be
machined as deeply as possible with the most robust possible tool.
The toolpaths calculated for the Clip option are used as the basis for the 3D Rework Machining cycle.
An area is determined and graphically displayed within the 3D Automatic Rest Machining cycle. Any further
machining occurs within the following cycle only: 3D Automatic Rest Machining.
When the Collision avoidance function is used, a milling area that is not within the stock is also protected
against collisions. If the milling area that is outside of the stock only consists of perpendicular surfaces, no
collision avoidance takes place; instead, the milling path output is suppressed.

Contouring

to the surface, such as grooves, cut edges or engravings. Using optional synchronization lines, the tool
inclination can be manually adjusted locally.

Retract mode
The retract mode defines the Z level where the system executes horizontal infeed movements. The mode
set is valid for all machining directions (incl. approach, retract and return movement macros) and for the
profiles machined with them. Exception: Machining in zigzag mode without return macro.
Clearance distance (1): all retract and infeed movements are executed via the clearance distance. Starting
and end positions of an infeed movement in rapid are displaced in Z direction in order to guarantee a
collision-free linear infeed movement. The clearance distance is added to these positions.
Clearance plane (2): all retract and infeed movements are executed via the clearance plane.

Macros
Approach and retract macros are used to define the tool approach at the start point and the tool retraction
from the end point of the contour. This behavior can be defined manually or calculated automatically by
hyperMILL.
Ramp height: The ramp height can be specified for the approach macro. Prevents the tool from plunging
vertically into any rest material that may remain on the bottom of the workpiece (see section Macros, Using
the ramp as a plunge macro).

Additional surfaces: temporary safety surfaces to avoid unnecessary rapid travel movements. Surfa-
ces in the machining area that need to be known to perform a correct collision check.
Check tool
The tool check ensures that all of the components defined for the tool are protected from a possible
collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.
Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.
Tool check setup: the tool check settings are specified in this dialog box. For further information, see
section Tool check setup (page 722)
Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:

• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).
Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Angle difference for various tool inclinations between two separate machining areas
(for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance
distance is defined as the retract mode (Parameters dialog page) (1).
If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the
clearance distance (dialog page: Parameters) (2). If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to
clearance distance. If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to clearance distance.
Clearance straighten angle: If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of
the tool is greater than the defined straighten angle (default = 45°), the tool turns to the defined value for
the straighten angle, after it has reached the clearance plane.
If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of the tool is smaller than or
equal to the defined Straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
inclination (3).

Swarf Cutting two Curves
The cycle is used for regular surfaces that permit a milling tool to come into contact with a line. For swarf
cutting with two curves, the machining area in the axial direction is also defined by a profile curve.
As opposed to swarf cutting with one curve, the tool inclination here is defined by an additional profile
curve. The use of end mills with swarf machining enables short machining times.
Strategy
Profiles
Top curve (1): Defines the tool inclination.
Bottom curve (2): Defines the end of machining in the axial direction.

Synchronize toolpaths
Equal (1): The tool orientation follows the ISO lines of a regular surface that would be formed by both
curves.
Distance (2):The tool is oriented to the shortest distance from the lower to upper curve. In particular for
trimming geometries with constant wall thickness.
Synchronization lines: Using the synchronization lines, the curves can be subdivided into sections to which
these methods can be applied. In particular in connection with the Equal synchronization strategy.

Infeed

Additional axial distance: Additional toolpath distance in the axial direction.
Machining area
Total lateral infeed / Total axial infeed: Total infeed in lateral or axial direction over all milling paths.
Determines the lateral or axial machining area.
If the total lateral infeed / total axial infeed is not an integer multiple of the infeed, then the final infeed
will be smaller. This allows a reduced milling tool load for the final infeed and an improved surface quality
(Roughing with finishing pass).

The retract mode defines the Z level where the system executes horizontal infeed movements. The mode
set is valid for all machining directions (incl. approach, retract and return movement macros) and for the
profiles machined with them. Exception: Machining in zigzag mode without return macro.

and end positions of an infeed movement in rapid are displaced in Z direction in order to guarantee a
collision-free linear infeed movement. The clearance distance is added to these positions.

Shape Offset Roughing
Roughing of slightly curved surfaces with a uniform allowance, where the milling path follows the selected
drive surfaces. Bottom surfaces may be defined for machining, making individual adjustments possible.
Tool
The following tool types may be used: ball mill, end mill and bullnose end mill.
Strategy
Machining options
Pocket inside out: Material removal during roughing always takes place from inside to outside. Approach
from outside does not take place.
Axial sorting: Areas like corners or pockets are sorted axially and machined consecutively, so that empty
paths and machining times are reduced.
Mode
Part surface mode: The Drive surfaces (in the Geometry section) define the scope to be machined in terms
of lateral dimensions and specify the orientation of the tool. The vertical machining area is defined by
the Top and Bottom parameters (on the Parameters tab). Both values are relative and refer to the Drive
surfaces that form the zero point of the vertical machining area.
Drive surfaces: The Drive surfaces (mandatory) define the scope to be machined in terms of lateral
dimensions and specify the orientation of the tool. The vertical machining area is defined by the Top and
Bottom parameters (on the Parameters tab). Both values are relative and refer to a zero point that is
defined as follows:
1. Bottom surfaces are defined: The zero point corresponds to the Bottom surfaces if they are above
the Drive surfaces, including (positive or negative) offset. The zero point corresponds to the Drive
surfaces if the Bottom surfaces are below the Drive surfaces, including (positive or negative)
offset.
2. Bottom surfaces are not defined: The zero point corresponds to the Drive surfaces, including
(positive or negative) offset.
The following simplified graphic shows the connection between Drive and Bottom surfaces in the Drive
surfaces mode.
(1) Negative offset, (2) Positive offset, (3) Drive surface, (4) Zero point, (5) Bottom plane, (6) Drive surface
including offset, (7) Drive surface.

Invert: Machining takes place on the side opposite the normal to face.

Offset: Offset in the axial direction on the defined drive surfaces.

Toolpath fillets
In contour-parallel machining, the toolpaths can be rounded in the plane.
Radius for horizontal infeed (1): the horizontal infeed between the tool paths is executed with an approach
and departure radius.
Fillet radius (2): Abrupt changes in direction within the cutting toolpaths are rounded with the specified
radius.
Fillet all toolpaths (3): Corners of the model contour are rounded with the radius defined above so that the
machining contour deviates from the model contour at the outer corners.

Parameters
Machining area
The values for top and bottom are always with reference to the defined Drive or Bottom surfaces. The
parameters specify the machining area in the axial direction. For general information on the vertical
machining area, see the next section.
Infeed / allowance
Vertical stepdown (1): The vertical stepdown determines the number of machining planes.
Allowance (2): remaining material on the workpiece. Calculated in direction of the surface normals. Added
to the Clearance parameter during machining (see section Check tool).
For the 3D Arbitrary Stock Roughing cycle, the distance between the tool and the stock
and model is specified by the defined clearance only.
If the XY allowance is negative, end mills are not allowed.
If a bullnose end mill is used, the negative XY allowance must be smaller or equal to the tool radius minus
the corner radius.
Example: tool radius (5 mm) - corner radius (4 mm) = 1 mm.
The stock allowance only applies for surfaces. For areas where there are no surfaces present there will be
no stock allowance calculated.
Z constant machining: In the last machining level, the allowance only applies in X and Y direction, not in Z
direction. The specification of negative stock allowances is possible as long as the sum of (negative) stock
allowance and tool corner radius does not become negative. When specifying negative stock allowances,
surface gaps should not exceed the following maximum values (otherwise, risk of ‘nose-diving’): 2 x (tool
radius + negative allowance).
Additional allowance XY: Additional horizontal stock allowance enables machining with different stock
allowances for the bottom and side walls of the machining area.

High Performance
Note for users of the ‘High Performance Mode’ option in the Shape Offset Roughing
cycle, specifically for manufacturing components, in particular, bladed rotors (including
impellers and blisks), for turbomachines, aircraft and spacecraft).
Please note that this option may not be used without the consent of the patent holder
MTU Aero Engines AG to apply the patented method in accordance with EP1356886B1,
DE10219012B4, US6869259B2 or CA2425401C for the purpose of manufacturing com-
ponents for turbomachines, aircraft and spacecraft, in particular, bladed rotors (including
impellers and blisks).
For information on High Performance Mode, see section High Performance Roughing (page 825). The
Entry feedrate function is not available for 5X Shape Offset Roughing.
Boundary
The definition of the machining area using Boundary is supported. A boundary can be defined as closed
curves, such as polylines, splines or circles. The Z-position of the boundaries is not relevant to the
calculation of the machining area.
Tool reference
Machining of the defined area until the tool axis is on top of the boundary (1) . The tool axis can never
move beyond the boundary.
Offset: A positive value enlarges the boundary, while a negative value reduces it.
1
Macros
Approach macro
Ramp (A): Ramp-shaped plunging into material. Default if machining is not performed in High Performance
Mode. Use Angle (1) to specify the lead angle. The length of the approach movement, the clearance and
the max. axial lift are calculated automatically.
During the approach from the outside, the angle is considered and limited by the maximum axial lift. A
larger angle, thus, increases the probability that an approach from the outside is possible.
Helical (B): Preferred in High Performance Mode. Use Angle (1) to specify the lead angle of the helix. The
number of revolutions executed by the tool in the course of the infeed movement is computed from the
value of the vertical stepdown and the lead angle of the helix.

Plunge macro in High Performance Mode
The Spindle RPM and Dwell time parameters control the tool behavior for the plunge macro. Spindle
speed changes take place during the dwell time before and after the plunge macro.
Please ensure that your machine and postprocessor support this parameter.
Setup
Model
Specify the model (milling area) required for the current job.
Multiple allowances: If the milling area contains groups with different allowances, these allowances are
taken into account during machining if the function is enabled.
Additional surfaces: temporary safety surfaces to avoid unnecessary rapid travel movements. Surfa-
ces in the machining area that need to be known to perform a correct collision check.
Stock
The Enable stock option (see tab Settings) enables roughing with stock in the shape offset roughing cycle.
Enable Generate resulting stock option if a stock chain is to be created in multiple machining steps.
Both approach and retract movements, as well as the stepdown movements for the tracked stock, are
optimized.
To avoid problems in approach and retracting in flat areas, the machining tolerance
must be less than half of the axial infeed and less than 5% of the tool diameter in the
first job. If it is a stock chain, all stocks previously used should meet this condition.

collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.

define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the

For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:

• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).

Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Angle difference for various tool inclinations between two separate machining areas
(for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance
distance is defined as the retract mode (Parameters dialog page) (1).
If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the
clearance distance (dialog page: Parameters) (2). If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to
clearance distance. If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to clearance distance.
Clearance straighten angle: If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of
the tool is greater than the defined straighten angle (default = 45°), the tool turns to the defined value for
the straighten angle, after it has reached the clearance plane.
If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of the tool is smaller than or
equal to the defined Straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
inclination (3).

Tool
The following tool types can be used: Ballmill, Endmill, Bullnose endmill, Barrel cutter and Lollipop.
When using the Lollipop tool type, the level shape finishing cycle can be linked also within a linking job.
Warning: Undercut machining is not supported.
Reference → Corner rest mode
Available for the strategy Side walls.
Diameter: The reference diameter is composed of the tool diameter + 2x Fillet radius of the preceding
rouging operation. Use these values to define the proportion of the remaining rest material for the finishing.
The following applies: For machining to take place, the specified reference diameter must be greater than
the tool diameter + 2 * Fillet radius.
For further information on tool definitions, see sections Define tool and OPEN MIND tool database.
Strategy
Machining options
The following strategies are available to define the machining area for Finishing:
Edge only: (1) All lateral walls will be machined in a single axial infeed. The value of the parameter Top
(see dialog page Parameters → Machining area) will not be considered.
Bottom only: (2) All surfaces accessible from the point of view of the tool will be machined in a single
axial infeed. The value of the parameter Top (see dialog page Parameters → Machining area) will not be
considered.
CAM
1281

-- 1281 of 1632 --

Side walls: (3) All lateral walls will be machined in multiple axial infeeds (also see dialog page Parameters
→ Axial infeed).
Side walls and bottom: (4) All lateral walls will be machined in multiple axial infeeds (also see dialog page
Parameters → Axial infeed) along with all bottom surfaces.
Machining sequence
Axial sorting: Areas like corners or pockets are sorted axially and machined consecutively, so that empty
paths and machining times are reduced. Available for the Side walls and Side walls and bottom options.
Prefer spiral: Machining is performed in one continuous toolpath with a spiral-shaped vertical stepdown.
Only available if the Axial sorting function is enabled.
Allow zigzag: Machining occurs with an alternating orientation/cutting mode. Here, the machining mode
with the shortest total machining time is automatically used. Available for the Side walls and Side walls and
bottom options. The option does not affect closed toolpaths or bottom machining. Approach and retract
macros may be dropped in case of paths directly on top of each other.
Cutting mode
Climb milling, Conventional milling: In the case of contour-parallel machining with continuous orientation,
the following definitions apply: climb milling and conventional milling relate to clockwise rotating tools. To
perform climb milling with an anticlockwise rotating tool, select conventional milling. For climb milling with
tools rotating clockwise, the following machining directions apply:
(1) Outside machining in clockwise direction.
(2) Inside machining in counterclockwise direction.

Mode
Part surface mode: The Drive surfaces (in the Geometry section) define the scope to be machined in terms
of lateral dimensions and specify the orientation of the tool. The vertical machining area is defined by
the Top and Bottom parameters (on the Parameters tab). Both values are relative and refer to the Drive
surfaces that form the zero point of the vertical machining area.
Drive surfaces: The Drive surfaces (mandatory) define the scope to be machined in terms of lateral
dimensions and specify the orientation of the tool. The vertical machining area is defined by the Top and
Bottom parameters (on the Parameters tab). Both values are relative and refer to a zero point that is
defined as follows:
1. Bottom surfaces are defined: The zero point corresponds to the Bottom surfaces if they are above
the Drive surfaces, including (positive or negative) offset. The zero point corresponds to the Drive
surfaces if the Bottom surfaces are below the Drive surfaces, including (positive or negative)
offset.
2. Bottom surfaces are not defined: The zero point corresponds to the Drive surfaces, including
(positive or negative) offset.
The following simplified graphic shows the connection between Drive and Bottom surfaces in the Drive
surfaces mode.

Macros
Additional movements to vertical infeed and retract movements that define a gentle approach and retract
behavior at the calculated milling paths.
Macros are only executed if they do not result in a collision with neighboring surfaces.
Macro mode
Macros can be defined manually or calculated automatically by
hyperMILL.
Automatic
Smooth: The approach or retract movement is performed smoothly in a circular motion.
Length: Defines the length of the approach or retract movement.
Side clearance/Axial clearance: Clearance in the axial or X/Y direction that can be travelled without a
collision.
Max. axial lift: Maximum lifting movement in the axial direction.
Feedrate macros: Various feedrate values for approach and retract macros. Default = Feedrate XY.
Manual
The tool is approached or retracted either in a Perpendicular (1), Circular (2) or Tangential (3) manner.
The retraction can also be performed as a Ramp (4). These additional movements are only ever performed
if they do not result in a collision with neighboring surfaces.
The approach or retract movement is performed smoothly in a circular motion.

Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

Retract mode
Defines the Z level where retract movements are executed. A distinction is made between the following
retract movements:
• 3D retract movements to the next infeed plane or the next machining surface.
• 5X retract movements to change the tool orientation.
Clearance plane: All retract movements take place via the clearance plane.
Clearance distance: 3D retract movements take place via the clearance distance. 5X retract movements
take place via the clearance plane.
Production mode: 3D retract movements take place via the shortest possible link between the infeed
planes and the machining surfaces. 5X retract movements take place via the clearance plane.

allowed. The value 1 guides the tool on the upper contact point (1) of the barrel radius (2) on the surface.

The straighten angle must be defined so that the tip of the tool describes the deepest
point of the entire collision body, including spindle and head. The Z axis of the frame
must be parallel to the Z axis of the NCS.
Clearance feedrate: Linking movements between two machining areas in the clearance distance are
executed at this feedrate.
Condition for retraction to clearance plane:
Clearance plane is defined as retract mode or value for Clearance straighten angle is exceeded (as
described above).
NC parameters
Machining tolerance: Enter the required machining tolerance. The value defines the accuracy with which
the calculation for the generation of the toolpaths is carried out.
Maximum G1 length(1): maximum length of the G1 movements on planar surfaces which are output in
the NC program. Greater distances are subdivided into a corresponding number of G1 movements of the
specified length. Controlling the G1 length avoids too strong accelerations of the machine on large planar
surfaces.

Tangential finishing of curved surfaces. Definition of the contact point of the tool by automatically gen-
erated Iso curves or Z-constant curves. Selection of manually generated curves is optionally possible.
Collision avoidance and automatically generated approach and retract macros ensure optimal tool paths.

conical barrel tool.

Setup
Model
Check model: The CAD model is checked for possible changes to the parameters defined in the job.
Select the model (milling area) required for the current job.
Additional surfaces: temporary safety surfaces to avoid unnecessary rapid travel movements. Surfa-
ces in the machining area that need to be known to perform a correct collision check.
Check tool
The tool check ensures that all of the components defined for the tool are protected from a possible
collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.
Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.
Tool check setup: the tool check settings are specified in this dialog box. For further information, see
section Tool check setup (page 722)
Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

Display calculated tool length

hyperMILL is displayed. In this
instance, after creating the toolpath file(s), select the tool in the browser and choose the Usage function on
the shortcut menu.
For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:
• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).
Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Angle difference for various tool inclinations between two separate machining areas
(for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance
distance is defined as the retract mode (Parameters dialog page) (1).
If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the
clearance distance (dialog page: Parameters) (2). If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to
clearance distance. If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to clearance distance.
Clearance straighten angle: If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of
the tool is greater than the defined straighten angle (default = 45°), the tool turns to the defined value for
the straighten angle, after it has reached the clearance plane.
If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of the tool is smaller than or
equal to the defined Straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
inclination (3).

surfaces (C).
During the up movement, Feedrate → Up (3) and Feedrate → Up blending (4) are used. The feedrate Up
blending (4) applies in the area of the transition in which the tool moves away from the bottom surfaces

must be parallel to the Z axis of the NCS.

Additive Manufacturing
Converts any prior reference job into an additive toolpath. The cycle offers additive manufacturing specific
options for the peripheral and infill paths and also dedicated 5 axis options to control the deposition
process.

Additive profile

Strategy
Reference path sorting
Usually, the toolpath for milling strategies is created from top to bottom. In additive manufacturing, the
normal sequence of adding material is from bottom to top. Therefore, the sequence of the reference
toolpath must be re-ordered. The following methods are available for this purpose.
From bottom to top (1): Use this method to re-sort the sequence of the reference job toolpaths from bottom
to top.
Valid only if all movements of the reference job between two G0 movements are lying
on a frame parallel to the additive manufacturing job frame.
Invert sequence (2): Use this method to invert the sequence of the reference job toolpaths. The first path of
the reference toolpath becomes the last path of the additive toolpath.
None (3): The machining sequence (of the reference job) remains unchanged.

Check tool
The tool check ensures that all of the components defined for the tool are protected from a possible
collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.
Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.
Tool check setup: the tool check settings are specified in this dialog box. For further information, see
section Tool check setup (page 722)
Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:
• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.

Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Difference of angle value for different tool inclinations between two separate machin-
ing areas (for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance
distance is defined as the retract mode (Parameters dialog page) (1).
If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the
clearance distance (dialog page: Parameters) (2). If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to
clearance distance. If there is no angle change, the tool moves rapidly to clearance distance.
Clearance straighten angle: If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of
the tool is greater than the defined Straighten angle (default = 45°), the tool turns to the defined value for
the Straighten angle, after it has reached the clearance plane.
If the angle between the Z axis of the current machining frame and Z axis of the tool is smaller than or
equal to the defined Straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
inclination (3).

Tube Milling
The tube package cycles are used for the 5X Complete Machining of complex curved, undercut channels
with closed cross-sections.
The channels to be machined may have any number of surfaces of any shape. There are no special
requirements concerning the quality of these surfaces. Overlaps and gaps are permissible as long as they
do not affect the tolerance of the milled channel. Larger gaps, for example, through side holes, slots or
similar, should be closed.
Since the machining is performed with interpolation between a start plane and an end plane, the channels
should be sufficiently smooth at both ends. The course of the channel is determined by a central curve for
the center of the channel to be machined. The machining is calculated with interpolation between a start
plane and an end plane.
The package contains the following cycles:
• 5X Tube Roughing
• 5X Tube Finishing
• 5X Tube Rest Machining
• 5X Halfpipe Machining
Overview of cycles
Roughing (1)
Spiral depth infeed with subsequent machining of the respective plane (lateral infeed from the outside in).
Tools: lollipop and ball mill, free holder geometries are supported.

Strategy
Central curve
Central curve: The central curve describes the default machining behavior with regards to
• the orientation of the planes at the beginning and end of machining – perpendicular to the central
curve,
• the position of the planes at the beginning and end of machining – upper/lower end point of the
central curve,
• the (optional) tilt curve for orientation of the tool.
The central curve does not have to be positioned exactly in the center of the tube’s cross-section, nor does
it need to precisely mirror its curvature profile. However, it must
• be aligned from outside in (facing the depth infeed),
• be positioned within the path(s) of the tool center,
• not create any shaded areas – if possible.
(1) Tube wall, (2) Central curve, (3) Shaded area

Tube Roughing
The following functions are only available in the Tube Roughing cycle.
Lateral infeed strategy
There are two directions available for the lateral infeed inside each level.
Toward central curve: (A) The tool moves in a spiral along the surfaces of the tube to the next plane and
then removes the material in the direction of the central curve.
Away from central curve: (B) The tool moves along the central curve to the next plane and then removes
the material from the central curve in the direction of the surfaces of the tube.

Tube Finishing
The following functions are only available in the Tube Finishing cycle.
Strategy
The Spiral and Parallel machining strategies are only available in the Tube Finishing
and Tube Rest Machining cycles.

Include bottom
Optimized machining of channels that are closed at the bottom (for example, recesses with an undercut

Synchronize toolpaths
Synchronization curves
When finishing with a parallel machining strategy, synchronisation curves may be used optionally to
influence the path profiles. The first synchronisation curve determines the course of the first path. All
further synchronisation curves divide the cross-section into interpolation areas for path calculation and
define the path profile required here.

Synchronisation profiles may go beyond the machining area. They have to be posi-
tioned - from the central curve's POV - behind the path to be calculated.
Equal: Between two synchronisation curves, all plane cuts are divided into the same number of segments.
The end points of the part segments are linked across all sections to form parallel paths.
Distance: The synchronisation of the points in the individual plane cuts, which are linked to form a parallel
path, takes place at the shortest distance between the cuts.

5-axis parameters
Tilt strategy
5X simultaneous (A): Collisions with the shank are avoided by tilting the tool around the cutting middle
point. To be able to plunge as deeply as possible without any collision avoidance, the tool can be tilted
with the desired tilt angle in the direction of the Tilt curve.
Fixed 3D (B): The tool axis always corresponds to the Z axis of the frame. The orientation of the frame
allows the reachable depth to be influenced without any collision avoidance. In this tilt strategy, the tool is
shifted laterally in order to avoid collisions.

Approach macro / Retract macro
Approach macros are additional movements during infeed on the first milling path of a job, infeeds
between the milling paths via the clearance plane or clearance distance.
Retract macros are additional motions during retraction after the last milling path of a cycle, retraction for
horizontal stepover between the milling paths via the clearance plane or clearance distance. The following
approach macros are available depending on the machining cycle.

Additional surfaces: temporary safety surfaces to avoid unnecessary rapid travel movements. Surfa-

Check tool
The tool check ensures that all of the components defined for the tool are protected from a possible
collision with the CAD model on the basis of existing material. The tool check is only available if you have
defined a tool and also a model to be checked.
Check on: You must always enable this option if you want the tool to be checked for collisions. If the tool
check is not enabled, the tool used is shown in red in the graphic preview. When this check is enabled,
the defined clearance is used to check all of the components defined for the tool. We recommend that you
define the clearance so that it gets continuously larger, starting with the thick shank in the direction of the
spindle.
Tool check setup: the tool check settings are specified in this dialog box. For further information, see
section Tool check setup (page 722)
Calculate length
The Reduce and Extend options are available if a holder, extension or spindle is defined. Only the Reduce
option is available for all 5X cycles.
Extend (1): if there is a tool extension, holder or spindle collision,
hyperMILL will calculate a larger tool
reach, based on the tool reach defined for the tool. So, there is no limit to the maximum tool reach – the
maximum possible tool reach of a real tool is simply ignored! This is the preferred option if the selected
tool is available in different lengths (e.g., short, long, extra-long) and the length calculation has not yet
determined the suitable real tool for the assembly. In this case, the tool is merely a geometry description
with an unlimited shank length.
Reduce (2):
hyperMILL calculates the shortest possible collision-free tool reach, based on the defined tool
reach of the tool. This is the preferred option if you only want to calculate tool lengths that are also actually
possible for the tool selected in the assembly. In this assembly, you must select the maximum tool reach
as the tool reach.

For unresolvable collision
Unresolvable collisions may occur if:
• It is not possible to avoid a collision in 5X machining as a result of a change to the tool orientation.
• In 3D machining, it is not possible to resolve a collision involving the tool extension, holder and/or
spindle by extending the tool (see calculating the tool length) or a collision will occur with the thick
shank.
If a collision cannot be avoided by changing the tool orientation (5X) or tool length calculation, various
options are available for the machining strategies:
Stop: The toolpath calculation stops when a collision occurs (applies for all machining strategies).
Linking movement
Define the parameters for the linking movements between machining jobs with different frames.
Distance angle limit: Angle difference for various tool inclinations between two separate machining areas
(for example: drilling groups) of a model.
If the defined value (default = 91°) is exceeded or it is equal to the defined value, the linking movement
between the two machining areas takes place at the height of the clearance plane, even if Clearance

If the angle value falls below the defined value, the linking movement takes place at the height of the

equal to the defined Straighten angle, the tool moves to the clearance plane without changing the tool
